question: What were 'Chauth' and 'Sardeshmukhi' in the context of the Marathas?
option_3: Two taxes collected by the Marathas
option_4: Two titles given to the Peshwas
solution_text:
The correct answer is Two taxes collected by the Marathas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were two taxes levied by the Marathas, mainly on neighbouring non-Maratha territories (चौथ और सरदेशमुखी मराठों द्वारा वसूले जाने वाले दो कर थे)

 

• Chauth was one-fourth of the revenue of the area, and Sardeshmukhi was an additional tithe of 10 percent.

 

• These payments funded the Maratha army and secured a territory against Maratha raids.

 

• These revenue claims were an important source of income and also gave the Marathas a legal pretext for their expansion, as they extended their influence over territories belonging to the Mughals and the Deccan sultans.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sardeshmukhi was claimed as the hereditary right of the Maratha king as chief Deshmukh.

 

• Balaji Vishwanath obtained these rights from the Mughal court around 1719.

 

• Territories that paid were generally spared from Maratha plunder.

 

• The Mughal grant of these rights to the Marathas came in 1719 through the Sayyid brothers.

 

NOTE

 

• Two Maratha forts (Option 1): Forts such as Raigad, Purandar and Sinhagad were fortifications; Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were revenue demands, so they are not fort names.

 

• Two types of Maratha soldiers (Option 2): Maratha soldiers were classified as Paga horsemen and Silladars, among other groups, and the two words do not refer to cavalry or infantry categories.

 

• Two titles given to the Peshwas (Option 4): Peshwa and Chhatrapati were administrative and royal titles, while the terms in the question denote revenue demands imposed on territories outside Maratha control.

question: In Maratha society, the 'Kunbis' were:
option_4: Peasant-pastoralists who formed the backbone of the army
solution_text:
The correct answer is Peasant-pastoralists who formed the backbone of the army.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kunbis were a large community of peasant-pastoralists (farmers and cultivators) in Maratha society who provided the backbone of the Maratha army (कुनबी मराठा समाज के किसान-पशुपालक थे, जो सेना की रीढ़ थे)

 

• Shivaji's soldiers were mostly drawn from such farming families, which gave his army a strong local base.

 

• They are distinct from the priestly Chitpavan Brahmanas who later held the Peshwaship.

 

• Their position at the base of society explains why the army could be raised quickly in the monsoon-free season, as the farmers served in the military between cultivation seasons.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mavli infantry from the hills was recruited into Shivaji's army.

 

• Kunbis were later influenced by social-reform efforts in Maharashtra.

 

• The Maratha caste claimed Kshatriya descent in some contexts.

 

• The Kunbi category is also found in Gujarat and Karnataka under other local names.

 

• Kunbis are listed in the old Maratha rural hierarchy under the patil, the village headman, who often gave military recruits to the state.

 

NOTE

 

• Priests of the Chitpavan community (Option 1): The Chitpavan Brahmanas were a priestly and administrative community from which the Peshwas came; Kunbis were agricultural, so they were not priests.

 

• Merchant bankers (Option 2): Merchant bankers belonged to groups like the Marwari and Gujarati traders who financed rulers, and the Kunbis were cultivators with no role as financiers.

 

• The Mughal mansabdars (Option 3): Mansabdars were Mughal ranked officials appointed by the emperor and paid by grades, whereas the Kunbis were Maratha cultivators who also served in the Maratha army and farmed their lands.

question: After Shivaji's death, effective political power in the Maratha state gradually passed into the hands of the:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chitpavan Brahmana Peshwas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After Shivaji, power gradually passed to the Chitpavan Brahmana Peshwas, with the Peshwa becoming the real ruler from 1713 (शिवाजी के बाद सत्ता चितपावन ब्राह्मण पेशवाओं के हाथ में आई)

 

• Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao I and Balaji Baji Rao all belonged to this family and made the post hereditary.

 

• The Chhatrapati at Satara was reduced to a nominal king.

 

• The shift of power from the king to the Brahmin Peshwa family altered the political structure, since a king who had little real control over the treasury and army could not oppose the minister.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Peshwas were based in Pune.

 

• Chitpavans came from the Konkan region.

 

• The Bhonsle, Holkar, Scindia and Gaikwad chiefs formed a Maratha confederacy under the nominal leadership of the Peshwa.

 

• Shahu's death in 1749 left the Peshwa as the sole centre of government at Pune.

 

• A frequent question asks who really ruled after Shahu, and the answer is the Peshwa, because he controlled administration, finance and the army.

 

NOTE

 

• Mughals (Option 1): The Mughals were the opponents of the Marathas and never acquired power inside the Maratha state, which remained independent even during Aurangzeb's long war.

 

• Kunbi chiefs (Option 2): Kunbis formed the backbone of the army but did not govern; the effective political control moved to the Peshwa family and not to the farmer community.

 

• Adil Shahis (Option 4): The Adil Shahis of Bijapur were a rival Deccan sultanate whose rule ended in 1686, so they did not exercise authority in the Maratha polity afterwards.

question: The city of Ujjain expanded under the patronage of which Maratha chief?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sindhia.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ujjain developed and expanded under the patronage of the Sindhia (Scindia) rulers, founded by Ranoji Scindia (उज्जैन सिंधिया शासकों के संरक्षण में विकसित हुआ)

 

• The Scindias were Maratha generals of the Peshwa who gained control of Malwa and later made Gwalior their capital.

 

• Mahadaji Scindia, a notable ruler of the line, was the signatory on the Maratha side of the Treaty of Salbai in 1782.

 

• Scindia power in Ujjain began with Ranoji Scindia, who was appointed by the Peshwa to administer Malwa, and the town grew as a base for the Maratha rule in the region.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ujjain was the Scindia headquarters before Gwalior.

 

• The Holkars ruled Indore, the Gaikwads ruled Baroda and the Bhonsles ruled Nagpur.

 

• Mahadaji built a strong army with French-trained officers.

 

• Gwalior became the Scindia capital in the later eighteenth century.

 

• Ranoji Scindia started his career as a humble member of the Peshwa's household and rose as a general in Malwa.

 

NOTE

 

• Holkar (Option 1): The Holkars established themselves at Indore, a neighbouring city in Malwa, and are famous for Ahilyabai's patronage of temples and ghats, not Ujjain's expansion.

 

• Gaikwad (Option 2): The Gaikwads were the Maratha rulers of Baroda in Gujarat, quite distant from Malwa, so they did not patronise Ujjain's growth.

 

• Bhonsle (Option 3): The Bhonsles of Nagpur ruled in the east of Maharashtra and the Berar region, outside the Malwa area in which Ujjain lies.

question: From which decade did Maratha campaigns into Rajasthan put severe pressure on the principalities there and check their further expansion?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1740s.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Maratha expeditions into Rajasthan became severe from the 1740s, under the Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao and the Maratha sardars (1740 के दशक से मराठा अभियानों ने राजपूत रियासतों पर दबाव डाला)

 

• These raids and demands for chauth strained the Rajput states and checked their further territorial expansion.

 

• The period coincides with the weakening of the Mughal Empire after Nadir Shah's invasion in 1739.

 

• Maratha incursions took the form of raids that demanded tribute from Rajput states such as Jaipur, Jodhpur and Mewar, whose divisions made it difficult to unite against the invaders.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jaipur and Jodhpur were among the Rajput states pressured.

 

• Holkar and Scindia played a major role in the north.

 

• Rajput rulers often turned to the Marathas or the British for support afterwards.

 

• Maratha forces under Malhar Rao Holkar and Jayappa Scindia were involved in Rajasthan around the mid-eighteenth century.

 

NOTE

 

• 1560s (Option 2): The 1560s were the time of Akbar's conquests, including Chittor in 1568, when the Mughals pressed the Rajputs, and the Marathas were not a political force at all.

 

• 1620s (Option 3): The 1620s fall in Jahangir's reign and the early life of Shahaji; Maratha power in Rajasthan did not exist, since it was still a regional Deccan force.

 

• 1680s (Option 4): The 1680s were the time of Sambhaji's struggle against Aurangzeb in the Deccan, so Maratha energies were occupied in the south, and not in Rajasthan.

question: The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) was fought during the Governor Generalship of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Warren Hastings.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The First Anglo-Maratha War began in 1775 and ended in 1782, when Warren Hastings was the Governor General of Bengal (प्रथम आंग्ल-मराठा युद्ध वारेन हेस्टिंग्स के काल में 1775-82 तक चला)

 

• It was triggered by the British support for Raghunath Rao's claim to the Peshwaship, formalised in the Treaty of Surat of 1775.

 

• The war ended with the Treaty of Salbai in 1782, which brought nearly two decades of peace.

 

• Warren Hastings was the first holder of the title of Governor General of Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773, and the Maratha war was among his major challenges alongside the war with Mysore.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Warren Hastings was Governor General from 1773 to 1785.

 

• He is different from Lord Hastings (Marquess of Hastings), who held office from 1813 to 1823.

 

• The Maratha power was not fully broken in this first round.

 

• The Second Anglo-Mysore War also occurred in his period, in 1780-84.

 

• The Regulating Act of 1773 created the post of Governor General of Bengal, and Warren Hastings was the first to hold the office.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Wellesley (Option 1): Lord Wellesley served from 1798 to 1805 and is associated with the second war of 1803-06 and the subsidiary alliance, not with the first Anglo-Maratha war of the 1770s.

 

• Lord Hastings (Option 2): Lord Hastings, the Marquess of Hastings, governed in 1813-23 and presided over the third war of 1817-18, some four decades after the first war began.

 

• Lord Cornwallis (Option 3): Lord Cornwallis was Governor General in 1786-93 and again briefly in 1805; he is known for the Permanent Settlement and the Mysore war, and not for the first Maratha conflict.

question: The Treaty of Surat (1775) was signed between the British and:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Raghunath Rao.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Surat (1775) was concluded between Raghunath Rao (Raghoba) and the British of the Bombay presidency (सूरत की संधि 1775 में रघुनाथ राव और अंग्रेजों के बीच हुई)

 

• By it the Bombay presidency agreed to accept Raghunath Rao as Peshwa, which set off the First Anglo-Maratha War.

 

• In return the English expected territorial gains such as Salsette and Bassein.

 

• The agreement was a case of the British intervening in a succession dispute within the Marathas, as the Bombay government wanted Salsette and Bassein in return for backing a claimant.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Raghunath Rao, also called Raghoba, was the uncle of Peshwa Narayan Rao, whose posthumous son Madhava Rao II was the infant Peshwa.

 

• The Calcutta Council later disowned the treaty and made its own agreement at Purandar in 1776.

 

• Nana Phadnavis led the Peshwa's regency council in Pune opposing him.

 

• The British force that marched towards Pune was checked at Wadgaon in 1779.

 

NOTE

 

• Madhava Rao II (Option 1): Madhava Rao II was the infant Peshwa recognised by the Pune government and by the later treaties; he was the rival of Raghunath Rao, so he did not enter into this agreement.

 

• Mahadaji Scindia (Option 3): Mahadaji Scindia was the Maratha chief who negotiated the Treaty of Salbai of 1782 with Warren Hastings, seven years after the Surat agreement.

 

• Nana Phadnavis (Option 4): Nana Phadnavis was the chief minister of the Pune regency who opposed Raghunath Rao's claim, so he would never have recognised the Bombay arrangement of 1775.

question: Under the Treaty of Purandar (1776), which of the following was accepted?
option_1: Madhava Rao II as the new Peshwa
solution_text:
The correct answer is Madhava Rao II as the new Peshwa.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• By the Treaty of Purandar (1776) Madhava Rao II was accepted as the new Peshwa, and the British retained Salsette along with a heavy war indemnity (1776 की पुरंदर संधि में माधवराव द्वितीय को पेशवा माना गया)

 

• This treaty was negotiated by the Calcutta Council under Warren Hastings and cancelled the earlier Bombay arrangement of 1775.

 

• It must not be confused with the Treaty of Purandar of 1665 signed between Shivaji and Jai Singh.

 

• The Purandar treaty of 1776 was an attempt by the Calcutta authorities to settle the matter quickly and without the heavy demand that Bombay had made on Raghunath's behalf, while retaining a minimum of gains.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Bombay government repudiated this treaty and went to war again.

 

• The treaty of 1665 is also spelt Purander.

 

• Salsette is an island near Bombay and was strategically significant for the British.

 

• Raghunath Rao was granted a pension in the Calcutta arrangement.

 

• The treaty of 1776 should not be mistaken for the one concluded with Shivaji and Jai Singh in 1665, though both bear the same place name.

 

NOTE

 

• Raghunath Rao as the Peshwa (Option 2): Raghunath Rao was the claimant supported at Surat in 1775; the 1776 settlement rejected his claim and gave him only a pension, so he was not accepted as Peshwa.

 

• Tarabai as regent (Option 3): Tarabai belonged to the early eighteenth-century struggle over the throne and had nothing to do with the 1776 negotiation, which concerned the Peshwaship.

 

• Nana Saheb as the Peshwa (Option 4): Nana Saheb is the other name of Balaji Baji Rao, who died in 1761, fifteen years before this treaty, or the later adoptee of Baji Rao II, and neither can be the Peshwa of 1776.

question: The Treaty of Salbai (1782), which ended the First Anglo-Maratha War, was signed between:
option_1: Lord Wellesley and Daulat Rao Scindia
option_3: Lord Hastings and Baji Rao II
solution_text:
The correct answer is Warren Hastings and Mahadaji Scindia.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Salbai (1782) was concluded between Warren Hastings and Mahadaji Scindia, and it ended the First Anglo-Maratha War (सालबाई की संधि 1782 में वारेन हेस्टिंग्स और महादजी सिंधिया के बीच हुई)

 

• It came at the end of a series of battles, in which neither side secured a decisive victory.

 

• The British kept Salsette and a long period of peace followed, as Scindia acted as mediator and guarantor.

 

• Scindia's role as an intermediary, which allowed him to win recognition in British eyes as a great power, reflected the diplomatic skill of Mahadaji, and the treaty restored the situation at the time before the war except for Salsette.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Salbai is a village in present-day Madhya Pradesh.

 

• The treaty was ratified in 1783.

 

• Peace lasted till the second Anglo-Maratha war of 1803.

 

• The English returned the territories they had occupied during the war, other than Salsette and Broach.

 

• Salbai's terms also confirmed the Maratha claim to the territories held before the war, while the East India Company obtained an assurance about its trade.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Wellesley and Daulat Rao Scindia (Option 1): Wellesley and Daulat Rao Scindia are connected to the 1803 war and the Treaty of Surji Anjangaon, signed two decades after Salbai in the second conflict.

 

• Lord Hastings and Baji Rao II (Option 3): Lord Hastings and Baji Rao II belong to the third war, ending in the Treaty of Poona in 1817, almost thirty-five years after the peace of 1782.

 

• Raghunath Rao and Warren Hastings (Option 4): Raghunath Rao had been the British ally at Surat in 1775 and was sidelined in the settlement of 1782, so the treaty was not an agreement between him and Hastings.

question:
Consider the following statements about the First Anglo-Maratha War:

1. It began in 1775 under Warren Hastings.

2. It ended with the Treaty of Salbai.

3. It ended with the Treaty of Deogaon.

Which of the statements are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the war began in 1775 with Warren Hastings as Governor General (प्रथम आंग्ल-मराठा युद्ध 1775 में शुरू होकर 1782 में सालबाई संधि से समाप्त हुआ)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Treaty of Salbai (1782), signed by Hastings and Mahadaji Scindia, ended it.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the Treaty of Deogaon (1803) belongs to the second war, concluded with the Bhonsle of Nagpur under Lord Wellesley.

 

• The three statements test the order of the wars: Deogaon came in 1803, well after Salbai, and belongs to the war in which Arthur Wellesley and Lord Lake commanded British armies.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Treaty of Surat of 1775 preceded the war.

 

• The Treaty of Purandar of 1776 came in the middle.

 

• Deogaon (December 1803) was signed along with the Treaty of Surji Anjangaon with Scindia.

 

• Wellesley's brother, Arthur, later became the Duke of Wellington.

 

• Statement based questions on treaties often swap the war to which a treaty belongs, and Deogaon is a favourite substitute for Salbai.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): Including statement 3 with statement 2 gives a combination in which the Deogaon treaty is wrongly assigned to the first war, and it also omits the correct statement about the 1775 start.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Statements 1 and 3 together wrongly credit Deogaon as the closing treaty of the first war, while rejecting the correct Salbai conclusion, so the pair contradicts the facts.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Accepting all three requires believing that one war ended with two different treaties across two decades; Deogaon, however, dates from the 1803 war with Wellesley in office.

question: The Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-06) took place when the Governor General of Bengal was:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Wellesley.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Second Anglo-Maratha War of 1803-06 was fought when Lord Wellesley was Governor General of Bengal (द्वितीय आंग्ल-मराठा युद्ध लॉर्ड वेलेस्ली के काल में हुआ)

 

• All the Maratha forces were defeated, and various treaties were signed, so a larger part of Central India came under British control.

 

• The conflict grew out of Wellesley's policy of the subsidiary alliance, which the Peshwa accepted at Bassein in 1802.

 

• The war grew from Baji Rao II's flight from Holkar's army to the British at Bassein, where he accepted a subsidiary alliance in 1802, which the other chiefs saw as a surrender of Maratha independence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Wellesley also fought the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War and defeated Tipu Sultan in 1799.

 

• Arthur Wellesley, his brother, won at Assaye in 1803.

 

• Lord Lake won at Delhi and Laswari.

 

• Under a subsidiary alliance the ruler had to maintain a British force at his own cost.

 

• Wellesley's subsidiary alliance system was applied to Hyderabad in 1798 and Mysore in 1799 before it was extended to the Peshwa at Bassein.

 

NOTE

 

• Warren Hastings (Option 1): Warren Hastings was in office during the first war from 1775 to 1782, so he cannot have governed in 1803, more than a decade after he left India.

 

• Lord Dalhousie (Option 2): Lord Dalhousie was Governor General in 1848-56 and is known for the Doctrine of Lapse; he came decades after the second Maratha war and the Peshwas' downfall.

 

• Lord Hastings (Option 4): Lord Hastings governed from 1813 to 1823 and conducted the third war of 1817-18, which succeeded the second war and should not be mixed with it.

question:
Match the treaty with the Maratha power that signed it:

Column A: (a) Treaty of Deogaon (b) Treaty of Surji Anjangaon (c) Treaty of Rajghat

Column B: (i) Holkar (ii) Bhonsle of Nagpur (iii) Scindia
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Deogaon (1803) was with the Bhonsle of Nagpur, the Treaty of Surji Anjangaon was with Scindia, and the Treaty of Rajghat (1805) was with Holkar (देवगांव-भोंसले, सुर्जी अंजनगांव-सिंधिया, राजघाट-होल्कर)

 

• Thus the pairing is a-ii, b-iii and c-i.

 

• Together these treaties, signed during the Second Anglo-Maratha War under Wellesley, resulted in British control over a larger part of Central India.

 

• These treaties were distinct agreements, each negotiated with a separate chief rather than with a united Maratha government, which shows how the confederacy had broken up into rival houses.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Deogaon was signed in December 1803 with Raghuji Bhonsle II.

 

• Surji Anjangaon followed soon after, with Daulat Rao Scindia.

 

• Yashwant Rao Holkar was the Holkar chief.

 

• Under Deogaon the Bhonsle ceded Cuttack and the Berar region's western part to the British.

 

• Two of the three treaties, Deogaon and Surji Anjangaon, were signed within a fortnight of each other in December 1803.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i (Option 1): In this key Deogaon is attached to Scindia and Surji Anjangaon to the Bhonsle, which swaps the two 1803 treaties; Deogaon was with Nagpur while Surji Anjangaon was with Gwalior.

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-ii (Option 3): Assigning Deogaon to Holkar and Rajghat to Bhonsle is wrong, because Holkar signed Rajghat in 1805 and the Nagpur ruler signed at Deogaon in 1803.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iii (Option 4): Linking Surji Anjangaon with Holkar and Rajghat with Scindia mixes up two different chiefs; Scindia was the party at Surji Anjangaon and Holkar the party at Rajghat.

question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:

A. Treaty of Surat

B. Treaty of Salbai

C. Treaty of Deogaon

D. Treaty of Poona
solution_text:
The correct answer is A, B, C, D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Surat (1775) came first, followed by the Treaty of Salbai (1782), then the Treaty of Deogaon (1803), and finally the Treaty of Poona (1817) (सूरत 1775, सालबाई 1782, देवगांव 1803, पूना 1817)

 

• Surat started the first war and Salbai ended it.

 

• Deogaon belongs to the second war under Wellesley and Poona to the third war under Lord Hastings.

 

• The order places the treaties by war: Surat and Salbai in the first, Deogaon in the second and Poona in the third, which is a simple way to remember the sequence of the three wars.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gwalior (1817) and Mandasor (1818) were later treaties of the third war.

 

• Rajghat followed in 1805.

 

• The Peshwa lost his rank in 1818.

 

• The three wars lasted 1775-82, 1803-06 and 1817-18.

 

• The three treaties signed with the Peshwa, Scindia and Holkar in 1817-18 had the same effect of curbing Maratha sovereignty.

 

NOTE

 

• B, A, C, D (Option 1): This sequence puts Salbai (1782) before Surat (1775), which is impossible since Salbai ended the war that Surat had started.

 

• A, C, B, D (Option 2): Placing Deogaon before Salbai breaks the order between the first and second wars; the second war of 1803 came more than two decades after the peace of 1782.

 

• A, B, D, C (Option 3): The last two are swapped here, putting Poona before Deogaon, but the Treaty of Poona was in 1817, during the third war, after the 1803 Deogaon agreement.

question: In the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-18), against the British under Lord Hastings were:
option_1: Peshwa Baji Rao II with Holkar and Bhonsle
solution_text:
The correct answer is Peshwa Baji Rao II with Holkar and Bhonsle.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-18) Peshwa Baji Rao II, with the Holkar and the Bhonsle, fought against the British under Lord Hastings (तृतीय युद्ध में पेशवा बाजीराव द्वितीय, होल्कर और भोंसले अंग्रेजों के विरुद्ध थे)

 

• The Marathas were defeated, and the treaties of Poona (1817), Gwalior (1817) and Mandasor (1818) were signed.

 

• The war destroyed the Maratha confederacy and left the British supreme in western and central India.

 

• The Peshwa had chafed under the Treaty of Bassein, and his attack on the Residency at Pune in 1817 provoked war, in which the Maratha armies were beaten at Khadki, Sitabuldi and Mahidpur.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The battles of Khadki and Koregaon Bhima occurred in this war.

 

• Pindari raids led to British intervention.

 

• Bajirao II surrendered to Sir John Malcolm in 1818.

 

• Appa Saheb Bhonsle was defeated at Sitabuldi in Nagpur.

 

• The Peshwa's last stand was a series of defeats in 1817 and 1818, including the battle of Ashti, after which he fled.

 

NOTE

 

• Tarabai with Shahu (Option 2): Tarabai and Shahu fought each other in the civil war of 1707-10 and never opposed the British, who had barely established themselves in India at that early date.

 

• Raghunath Rao with Scindia (Option 3): Raghunath Rao was a figure of the first war in the 1770s, and he died in 1783, so he had no role in the conflict of 1817-18.

 

• Sambhaji with Rajaram (Option 4): Sambhaji and Rajaram were Shivaji's sons who struggled against the Mughals in 1680-1700, over a century before the British fought the third war.

question:
Match the treaty with the party that it was signed with:

Column A: (a) Treaty of Poona (1817) (b) Treaty of Gwalior (1817) (c) Treaty of Mandasor (1818)

Column B: (i) Holkar (ii) Peshwa (iii) Scindia
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Poona (1817) was signed with the Peshwa, the Treaty of Gwalior (1817) with Scindia, and the Treaty of Mandasor (1818) with Holkar (पूना-पेशवा, ग्वालियर-सिंधिया, मंदसौर-होल्कर)

 

• That gives the combination a-ii, b-iii, c-i.

 

• These agreements accompanied the end of the third war and the collapse of Maratha independence.

 

• These three agreements, though signed in the context of one war, were negotiated individually, with Holkar's the last, and each curtailed the sovereignty of its signatory.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Under the Treaty of Poona the Peshwa gave up his claim over the Maratha confederacy.

 

• Mandasor was signed in January 1818 after the battle of Mahidpur.

 

• Scindia accepted British terms at Gwalior while the war was ongoing.

 

• After 1818 the Holkar and Scindia states survived as princely states under British paramountcy.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i (Option 1): This version attaches Poona to Scindia and Gwalior to the Peshwa, which reverses the actual parties: Poona was the Peshwa's treaty and Gwalior was Scindia's.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iii (Option 3): Here Poona is with the Peshwa but Gwalior with Holkar and Mandasor with Scindia; the last two are swapped, as Mandasor was with Holkar and Gwalior with Scindia.

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-ii (Option 4): Linking Poona with Holkar and Mandasor with the Peshwa is incorrect, since the Peshwa's treaty was Poona and the Holkar's treaty was Mandasor.

question:
Consider the following statements about the end of the Peshwa rule:

1. The Peshwa Baji Rao II surrendered to the British in 1818.

2. The British granted him a pension and abolished the post of Peshwa.

3. The British accepted his adopted son Nana Saheb as the next Peshwa.

Which of the statements are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Baji Rao II surrendered to the British in 1818, ending Peshwa rule (1818 में बाजीराव द्वितीय के आत्मसमर्पण से पेशवाई समाप्त हुई)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the British started a pension for him, and the position of Peshwa was abolished.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: Baji Rao II had no son and adopted Nana Saheb, but the British did not accept him as the next Peshwa and stopped giving the pension.

 

• The British thus used the final war to remove the one Maratha office around which the confederacy had been organised, annexing the Peshwa's territories to the Bombay Presidency.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The pension was around eight lakh rupees a year.

 

• Baji Rao II lived at Bithur near Kanpur until his death in 1851.

 

• The Satara kingdom was later annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse in 1848.

 

• The Peshwa's territory became a part of the Bombay Presidency under Mountstuart Elphinstone.

 

• Peshwa Baji Rao II was permitted to spend his remaining years at Bithur in present-day Uttar Pradesh.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): This pair accepts statement 3, which is false because the British refused to recognise Nana Saheb as Peshwa, and it drops the correct statement about the 1818 surrender.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Statements 1 and 3 together include the false claim of British acceptance of the adopted heir, while omitting the true fact that the Peshwa's post was abolished and a pension started.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): All three cannot hold, because the British did the opposite of statement 3; they stopped the pension and refused the adoption as part of the policy of ending the Peshwa line.

question: Nana Saheb, the adopted son of the last Peshwa Baji Rao II, later became one of the leaders of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Revolt of 1857.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adopted son of Baji Rao II, Nana Saheb, became one of the leaders of the Revolt of 1857, after the British refused him the pension and title (नाना साहेब 1857 के विद्रोह के प्रमुख नेता बने)

 

• Baji Rao II had no son, so he adopted Nana Saheb, but the British did not accept him as the next Peshwa.

 

• He led the rebels at Kanpur, with Tantia Tope as his able general.

 

• The 1857 episode shows how the British decisions about pensions and succession, especially the refusal of such rights to adopted heirs, produced anger among displaced ruling families.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nana Saheb's real name was Dhondu Pant.

 

• The policy of denying him the pension is cited as a cause of the revolt.

 

• The earlier Peshwa Nana Saheb (Balaji Baji Rao) is a different person.

 

• Nana Saheb is believed to have vanished from history around 1859 into Nepal.

 

• Tantia Tope was a close associate of Nana Saheb, who rose from his service at Bithur and led rebel armies in 1857.

 

NOTE

 

• The Third Battle of Panipat (Option 1): The Third Battle of Panipat was in 1761, nearly a century before the adopted son became active, and the earlier Peshwa of the same nickname led the Maratha side then.

 

• The Treaty of Salbai (Option 2): The Treaty of Salbai was signed in 1782, long before the adopted son of Baji Rao II was even born, so he could not be linked with it.

 

• The Second Anglo-Maratha War (Option 4): The Second Anglo-Maratha War ran from 1803 to 1806 and ended with the Treaties of Deogaon and Rajghat, while the heir of Baji Rao II emerged as a rebel in 1857.

question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:

A. Shivaji's coronation at Raigarh

B. Treaty of Purandar

C. Release of Shahu by Bahadur Shah I

D. Death of Sambhaji
solution_text:
The correct answer is B, A, D, C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Purandar came in 1665, followed by Shivaji's coronation at Raigarh in 1674, the death of Sambhaji in 1689, and the release of Shahu in 1707 (क्रम: पुरंदर 1665, राज्याभिषेक 1674, संभाजी की मृत्यु 1689, शाहू की रिहाई 1707)

 

• Each event follows the career of the early Marathas, from Shivaji's struggle to the Mughal captivity of Shahu.

 

• The release of Shahu in 1707 was the beginning of the Peshwa-led phase.

 

• The sequence covers more than forty years: Purandar was in the early part of Shivaji's career, the coronation was its high point, and the other two events concern the later wars with Aurangzeb.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shivaji died in 1680, between the coronation and Sambhaji's death.

 

• Rajaram's rule from 1689 to 1700 followed Sambhaji's death.

 

• Balaji Vishwanath became Peshwa in 1713.

 

• Aurangzeb died in 1707 within a few months of Shahu's release.

 

• Chronology based on the Maratha rulers' timeline is a good way to answer such questions quickly, using the key dates 1665, 1674, 1689 and 1707.

 

NOTE

 

• A, B, D, C (Option 1): Putting the coronation before the Treaty of Purandar inverts 1674 and 1665; Shivaji had to accept the Mughal treaty a decade before he assumed the title Chhatrapati.

 

• B, A, C, D (Option 3): In this sequence Shahu's release comes ahead of the death of Sambhaji, but Shahu was freed in 1707 as an outcome of Aurangzeb's death, eighteen years after Sambhaji's killing.

 

• B, D, A, C (Option 4): This order puts Sambhaji's death in 1689 before the coronation of 1674, which is chronologically impossible as the coronation of Shivaji preceded his son's end.

question: Which of the following sequences correctly lists the rulers of the Maratha state in order?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shivaji, Sambhaji, Rajaram, Shahu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sequence runs from Shivaji (founder, d. 1680) to Sambhaji (1680-89), then Rajaram (1689-1700), and finally Shahu, who became Chhatrapati after 1707 (क्रम: शिवाजी, संभाजी, राजाराम, शाहू)

 

• Sambhaji won the war of succession with Rajaram in 1680 and was succeeded by Rajaram after his execution in 1689.

 

• Tarabai acted as regent for her son between 1700 and 1707, before Shahu's accession with the help of Balaji Vishwanath.

 

• The sequence also shows that Rajaram and Tarabai, who are not named in the question, fill the gap between Sambhaji and Shahu, and so Shahu's rule is dated from the early eighteenth century.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shahu ruled from Satara.

 

• Tarabai's line ruled from Kolhapur.

 

• Shahu died in 1749.

 

• Shahu's reign is dated from 1707 to 1749.

 

• The order of Maratha heads is a typical objective question, where Tarabai and Shahu are sometimes added as distractors to confuse students.

 

• Maratha rulers after Shivaji, namely Sambhaji and Rajaram, were both his sons, but from different mothers.

 

NOTE

 

• Shivaji, Rajaram, Sambhaji, Shahu (Option 1): In this sequence Rajaram precedes Sambhaji, but Sambhaji won the succession dispute in 1680 and ruled until 1689, whereas Rajaram took charge only after that.

 

• Sambhaji, Shivaji, Rajaram, Shahu (Option 2): This arrangement puts Sambhaji ahead of Shivaji, which is impossible since Shivaji was the founder and Sambhaji's father; the first ruler had to be Shivaji.

 

• Shivaji, Sambhaji, Shahu, Rajaram (Option 4): Placing Shahu ahead of Rajaram fails because Shahu was a Mughal captive until 1707 while Rajaram led the Marathas from 1689 to 1700.

question:
Assertion (A): After Balaji Vishwanath, the Chhatrapati became a nominal king among the Marathas.

Reason (R): Real power came to lie with the Peshwa, the Principal Minister of the Maratha administration.

Choose the correct option.
option_1: Assertion and Reason are both true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
option_2: The Assertion is true but the Reason is false
option_3: The Assertion is false but the Reason is true
option_4: Assertion and Reason are both true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
solution_text:
The correct answer is Assertion and Reason are both true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true, and R explains A: from 1713, with Balaji Vishwanath, the Peshwa held real power, so the Chhatrapati was a nominal king (पेशवा के पास वास्तविक सत्ता आ गई और छत्रपति नाममात्र का राजा रह गया)

 

• The Peshwa was the Principal Minister of the Maratha administration and later the hereditary head of the state.

 

• Shahu, helped by Balaji Vishwanath, became Chhatrapati and depended on the Peshwa.

 

• The change was therefore structural: the Chhatrapati's authority continued in form, but the treasury, the army and political decisions were in the hands of the Peshwa and his officers in Pune.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Peshwa office continued until 1818.

 

• The Chhatrapati was based at Satara while the Peshwa governed from Pune.

 

• The Peshwa also led the military campaigns of the confederacy.

 

• The Peshwa's tenure was approved by the Chhatrapati through a formal investiture.

 

• Assertion-reason questions like this usually take a well-known fact about the Peshwa and ask whether the explanation is correct, with this case answered by the first option.

 

NOTE

 

• Assertion and Reason are both true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion (Option 1): Calling R a mere unrelated truth is wrong: the shift of effective authority to the Peshwa is the reason that the king's role shrank to a nominal one.

 

• The Assertion is true but the Reason is false (Option 2): A is not true-and-R-false: R is accurate, since the Peshwa was the Principal Minister and indeed held effective power after Balaji Vishwanath, so it is not a false reason.

 

• The Assertion is false but the Reason is true (Option 3): A cannot be false, because the notes of Maratha history clearly record the Chhatrapati as a nominal king after 1713, and R is likewise valid, so a combination rejecting A fails.

question:
Assertion (A): Shivaji refused to accept the Treaty of Purandar after his visit to Agra in 1666.

Reason (R): He was insulted by being made to wait at Aurangzeb's court and was then held captive.

Choose the correct option.
option_1: Assertion and Reason are both true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
option_2: Assertion and Reason are both true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
option_3: The Assertion is true but the Reason is false
option_4: The Assertion is false but the Reason is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Assertion and Reason are both true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: at the Mughal court at Agra Fort in 1666 Shivaji was insulted and held captive, so he refused to accept the Treaty of Purandar (आगरा में अपमान और बंदी बनाए जाने के बाद शिवाजी ने संधि नहीं मानी)

 

• Aurangzeb had made him wait among lesser nobles, which Shivaji took as a deep personal affront.

 

• The Treaty of 1665 had required him to give up 23 of 35 forts and send his son to the Mughal service, and the dishonour broke the understanding.

 

• The incident shows the importance of personal honour in Mughal-Maratha dealings, and Aurangzeb's decision to treat Shivaji as an ordinary mansabdar of the lowest rank proved to be a serious political error.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shivaji's escape from Agra took place in 1666.

 

• He resumed war and regained forts soon afterwards.

 

• Jai Singh died in 1667 on his return from the Deccan.

 

• Shivaji returned to Raigarh by December 1666.

 

• The Agra visit of 1666 and the Treaty of Purandar of 1665 are often asked together, as the fact that he refused the treaty after Agra is a favourite point.

 

NOTE

 

• Assertion and Reason are both true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion (Option 1): The reason is not just an incidental truth; the humiliation and captivity directly produced his refusal, so describing R as a non-explanation fails.

 

• The Assertion is true but the Reason is false (Option 3): Calling R false is wrong since historical accounts record that Shivaji was insulted at the court and detained; both lines are accurate historically.

 

• The Assertion is false but the Reason is true (Option 4): A is plainly true, since Shivaji repudiated the Purandar terms after 1666, and a claim that the assertion is false while the reason is true therefore misreads events.

question:
Assertion (A): The Marathas fought the Third Battle of Panipat against Ahmad Shah Abdali in 1761.

Reason (R): When Abdali invaded India, the responsibility of protecting the country fell on the Marathas.

Choose the correct option.
option_1: Assertion and Reason are both true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
option_2: The Assertion is true but the Reason is false
option_3: The Assertion is false but the Reason is true
option_4: Assertion and Reason are both true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
solution_text:
The correct answer is Assertion and Reason are both true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements hold, and R gives the reason: Abdali's invasion made it the duty of the Marathas to defend India, so they fought him at Panipat in 1761 under Balaji Baji Rao (अब्दाली के आक्रमण पर रक्षा का उत्तरदायित्व मराठों पर था)

 

• The Marathas fought very bravely, though they were defeated in the battle.

 

• Their position as the strongest power in north India after the decline of the Mughals made them the natural opponent of the Afghan invader.

 

• The Third Battle of Panipat was therefore a clash between a regional power that wished to establish a northern empire and an Afghan ruler summoned by Rohilla and Awadh leaders to resist it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Maratha commander was Sadashivrao Bhau, the Peshwa's cousin.

 

• Vishwasrao, the Peshwa's son, also died in the battle.

 

• The defeat damaged but did not end Maratha power, which revived under Mahadaji Scindia.

 

• Ahmad Shah Abdali was the ruler of the Durrani Empire of Afghanistan.

 

• The battle of Panipat is classified as a third battle, the first being in 1526 between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi and the second in 1556 between Akbar's army and Hemu.

 

NOTE

 

• Assertion and Reason are both true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion (Option 1): Describing R as not an explanation is mistaken since the Maratha duty to counter the Afghan invader is exactly why they confronted him at Panipat.

 

• The Assertion is true but the Reason is false (Option 2): R is not false; the Marathas did take up the defence of India against Abdali's invasion, and the 1761 battle shows this, so labelling the reason incorrect misreads events.

 

• The Assertion is false but the Reason is true (Option 3): A is true because the Third Battle of Panipat did occur in 1761 between these two sides, so a choice that rejects the assertion contradicts the established date.

question: Which of the following is NOT a treaty associated with the Anglo-Maratha wars?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Treaty of Amritsar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Amritsar (1809) was signed between the British and Ranjit Singh of the Sikhs, and it fixed the Sutlej as the boundary, so it is not a Maratha treaty (अमृतसर की संधि 1809 में रणजीत सिंह और अंग्रेजों के बीच हुई)

 

• Salbai (1782) ended the first war, Deogaon (1803) belonged to the second war, and Mandasor (1818) was a treaty of the third war.

 

• Hence three of the options are Anglo-Maratha treaties, and only one concerns the Punjab.

 

• The Treaty of Amritsar was meant to stop Ranjit Singh's expansion south of the Sutlej, and it has no link to the Marathas, whose conflicts with the British were settled at Salbai, Deogaon and the other treaties.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Charles Metcalfe negotiated the Amritsar treaty on behalf of the British.

 

• The treaty was signed under Lord Minto's government.

 

• Mandasor was signed with Holkar.

 

• Ranjit Singh's kingdom was based at Lahore.

 

• Three of the four wars between the British and the Marathas were fought between 1775 and 1818, and they are the central way of dating these treaties.

 

NOTE

 

• Treaty of Salbai (Option 1): Salbai was the 1782 treaty between Warren Hastings and Mahadaji Scindia, which closed the first Anglo-Maratha War, so it is an authentic Maratha-war treaty.

 

• Treaty of Deogaon (Option 2): Deogaon was signed with the Bhonsle of Nagpur in December 1803 during the second war under Wellesley, so it clearly belongs to the Maratha conflicts.

 

• Treaty of Mandasor (Option 4): Mandasor of January 1818 was imposed on Holkar at the end of the third war, thereby forming part of the Maratha settlement with the British.

question: Which of the following was NOT a Peshwa of the Maratha Empire?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shahu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Shahu (Shahuji) was a Chhatrapati, the king and grandson of Shivaji, not a Peshwa, since the Peshwa was the Principal Minister (शाहू छत्रपति थे, पेशवा नहीं)

 

• Balaji Vishwanath (1713-20), Baji Rao I (1720-40) and Balaji Baji Rao (1740-61) were the first three Peshwas.

 

• Shahu was freed in 1707 and relied on Balaji Vishwanath, who made him Chhatrapati.

 

• The difference between king and minister is a frequent source of confusion: Shahu was in the line of Shivaji, whereas the Peshwas were Chitpavan Brahmins who were ministers of the king.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shahu ruled from Satara until 1749.

 

• He appointed Balaji Vishwanath as Peshwa in 1713.

 

• He was the son of Sambhaji.

 

• The Peshwa family belonged to the Bhat surname.

 

• Shahu was himself the king who appointed the Peshwa, and Balaji Vishwanath was the first holder of the post to be appointed by him in 1713.

 

• The distinction between the Chhatrapati and the Peshwa appears often in questions on the later Maratha polity.

 

NOTE

 

• Balaji Vishwanath (Option 2): Balaji Vishwanath was the first Peshwa from 1713 to 1720, so he does belong to the list of Peshwas and cannot be the odd one out.

 

• Baji Rao I (Option 3): Baji Rao I was the second Peshwa, serving from 1720 to 1740, and fought about 41 battles; thus he is certainly a Peshwa.

 

• Balaji Baji Rao (Option 4): Balaji Baji Rao, also known as Nana Saheb, was the third Peshwa and held the office from 1740 to 1761, until the Panipat disaster.

question: When Raja Jai Singh of Amber besieged Shivaji, which fort did Shivaji hold where his family and treasure had been lodged?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Purandar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Jai Singh succeeded in besieging the Purandar fort, where Shivaji had lodged his family and treasure, and this forced him to negotiate the Treaty of Purandar (1665) (जयसिंह ने पुरंदर किले को घेरा जहाँ शिवाजी का परिवार और खजाना था)

 

• The siege made resistance impossible, so Shivaji opened negotiations with the Mughal general.

 

• The treaty required him to give up 23 of his 35 forts.

 

• Purandar and its twin fort Vajragad were the key positions in the siege, and the Mughal forces under Dilir Khan took Vajragad before attacking Purandar, which made Shivaji's resistance hopeless.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Purandar lies about 30 km from Pune.

 

• Sambhaji was born at Purandar in 1657.

 

• Shivaji's commander Murarbaji Deshpande died defending it.

 

• The fort is situated in the Sahyadri hills in the present-day Pune district.

 

• Questions about Purandar are common because it appears in two different contexts, the siege of 1665 and the second Purandar treaty of 1776.

 

NOTE

 

• Sinhagad (Option 1): Sinhagad, once called Kondhana, was later captured by Tanaji Malusare in 1670, and it was not the fort whose siege forced the 1665 settlement with the Mughals.

 

• Raigarh (Option 2): Raigarh was made the capital and was the site of the coronation in 1674, which came after the treaty and was unconnected with the siege by Jai Singh.

 

• Shivneri (Option 4): Shivneri is the fort of Shivaji's birth near Junnar, and it was not the Purandar stronghold besieged by the Mughal army where his dependants were kept.
